name: Ankle Sprain
secondary_queries: how long does a sprained ankle take to heal
seo_title: Ankle Sprain Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Ankle sprain treatment in North Palm Beach: guided weight bearing, strength and balance training to lower the risk of another sprain. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: A rolled ankle usually heals best with a plan, and structured rehab for motion, strength and balance can lower your chance of spraining it again.
what_it_is: Your ankle is held together by strong bands of tissue called ligaments. A sprain happens when the foot rolls, twists or lands awkwardly and those ligaments stretch or tear. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, around 90% of ankle sprains are inversion injuries, where the foot rolls inward and strains the ligaments on the outside of the ankle.

Sprains are graded by severity. A grade 1 sprain stretches the ligament, a grade 2 partly tears it, and a grade 3 tears it completely. A 2019 review in the Journal of Athletic Training estimates about 2 million acute ankle sprains happen in the United States each year. Athletes are at high risk, but a curb, a pothole or an uneven sidewalk can do it too.
symptoms: Pain, especially when you put weight on the foot
Tenderness when the ankle is touched
A popping feeling or sound at the moment of injury
A sense that the ankle is unstable or may give out
causes: Rolling the foot on an uneven surface, curb or hole
Sports with jumping, cutting or quick changes of direction
Poor balance, weak ankles or limited flexibility
Footwear that is worn out or wrong for the activity

how_therapy_helps.intro: The 2021 APTA clinical practice guideline for lateral ankle sprains, published in JOSPT, recommends protecting the ankle with a brace or tape while gradually increasing weight bearing, along with a structured exercise program covering motion, neuromuscular control and balance. It also supports manual therapy to reduce swelling and restore pain-free movement. After a first sprain, the guideline gives its highest grade to balance-focused exercise combined with bracing to reduce the risk of another sprain.
methods: Guidance on how much to load the ankle and when, with bracing or crutch advice matched to the grade of your sprain and your stage of healing.
Manual therapy for swelling and stiffness
Hands-on soft tissue and joint mobilization within a pain-free range to ease swelling and restore the ankle's upward bend for normal walking.
Early range of motion work that progresses to strengthening the muscles that support the ankle, done in the clinic and at home.
Single-leg balance drills that get harder over time, retraining the ankle's ability to sense and correct a roll before it becomes a sprain.
A staged return to walking, work and sport, including advice on whether a brace makes sense during higher-risk activities.

first_visit: Your first visit takes about an hour, and treatment begins the same day. Your therapist asks how the ankle rolled and whether you could walk afterward, then checks swelling and bruising, feels along the ligaments, measures ankle motion and tests stability. Watching you stand, walk and balance shows how the ankle is coping. Your therapist also screens for signs of a fracture that would need a physician's review first.
recovery: Recovery depends on the grade. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says rehab may take about 2 weeks for minor sprains and up to 6 to 12 weeks for more severe injuries, and APTA's ChoosePT guide notes that a complete ligament tear can take nine months to a year to heal fully. Pain often settles before balance and strength have fully returned. The JOSPT guideline cites a study in which 40% of people seen for a first sprain went on to develop chronic ankle instability, which is one reason to finish the balance work.
self_care: For the first two to three days, protect and rest the ankle and keep it raised on a pillow when you can.
Apply a wrapped ice pack for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours during those first days, as the NHS advises.
Avoid heat, alcohol and massage for the first couple of days.
Wrap a compression bandage around the ankle for support.
Return to walking as pain allows; the NHS suggests avoiding strenuous exercise such as running for up to 8 weeks.
see_a_doctor: You heard a crack at the time of injury, or the ankle looks misshapen or points at an odd angle
You cannot put any weight on the foot or walk more than a few steps
Numbness or tingling, or skin below the injury that turns blue or grey or feels cold to the touch
Large or worsening swelling or bruising, or a very high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery
Swelling or pain that is still present several weeks later despite care

faqs.q: Should I walk on a sprained ankle?
faqs.a: For a sprained ankle, the JOSPT clinical practice guideline recommends gradually increasing weight bearing while using a brace or tape for support, with the amount based on severity and pain. The NHS advises resting the ankle for the first few days. If you cannot put any weight on it or walk more than a few steps, get urgent medical care before starting rehab.

faqs.q: Is it better to wrap or brace a sprained ankle?
faqs.a: The 2021 JOSPT guideline gives its highest grade to using external support, such as a brace or tape, after an acute ankle sprain. The best choice depends on the grade of the sprain, the stage of healing, your pain and your preference. A compression bandage helps with swelling early on, and a therapist can help you choose support that fits your stage of healing.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my ankle is sprained or broken?
faqs.a: Sprains and fractures can look alike, and only an examination, sometimes with an X-ray, can tell them apart. The NHS advises emergency care if you heard a crack when you were injured, the ankle looks misshapen, or the foot is numb, tingling, blue or grey, or cold to the touch. Being unable to walk more than a few steps also needs prompt medical assessment.

faqs.q: Why does my ankle keep rolling after a sprain?
faqs.a: Repeat ankle rolling after a sprain is common. A 2019 review in the Journal of Athletic Training found that 40% of people developed chronic ankle instability one year after a first lateral ankle sprain, and a past sprain is one of the strongest risk factors for another. Lost balance and position sense often play a part, which is why balance training is a core part of rehab.

faqs.q: When can I play sports after an ankle sprain?
faqs.a: Return to sport after an ankle sprain depends on the grade and on how well your strength, balance and agility have come back, not on a fixed date. The JOSPT guideline supports a planned return with a brace used early on. APTA's ChoosePT guide recommends specific balance and strength exercises several times a week for up to a year to help prevent reinjury.

faqs.q: Do I need physical therapy for a mild ankle sprain?
faqs.a: Many mild ankle sprains improve with early self-care, and some people recover fully on their own. Physical therapy is worth considering if you are still limping after a week or two, the ankle feels wobbly, or you play sports. The JOSPT guideline recommends structured exercise and balance training after a sprain, and a past sprain is a strong risk factor for another.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 S93.4 (sprain of ankle) is a non-billable parent. S93.40- (unspecified ligament) children verified on icd10data.com; ligament-specific subcodes (S93.41- calcaneofibular, S93.42- deltoid, S93.43- tibiofibular) exist but were not shown on the fetched page. Requires 7th character.

Healing ranges differ by source: AAOS gives about 2 weeks for minor and 6 to 12 weeks for severe sprains; ChoosePT gives 2 weeks to 2 months (grade 1), 6 to 12 weeks (grade 2), 9 months to 1 year (grade 3). Only the AAOS range and the ChoosePT grade 3 figure are used in the body.
The 40% chronic instability figure is from Doherty et al as cited in both the JOSPT CPG and the Herzog 2019 review.
Self-care uses NHS PRICE/HARM wording (UK source). NHS says avoid running 'for up to 8 weeks'; confirm this fits your messaging.
First-visit fracture screening: no specific decision rule (e.g., Ottawa ankle rules) is named because it was not in the fetched sources.
